title: Stationary Two-Ball Dribble
description: Lock in and get comfortable with a ball in each hand. This foundational drill builds independent hand coordination and forces your weak hand to keep up with your strong hand. The player who can dribble two balls without looking down is already ahead of 90% of the gym.
coachingPoints: Keep your eyes up — never watch the ball. Pick a spot on the wall and stare at it.
Dribble to waist height with both hands moving in rhythm, then try alternating.
Stay in an athletic stance: knees bent, back straight, weight on the balls of your feet.
If you lose one ball, reset quickly. Composure under pressure starts in practice.

title: Figure-8 Dribble (Slow)
description: Thread the ball through your legs in a figure-8 pattern and feel every part of the ball in your fingertips. This drill is about control, not speed — mastering the slow version is what unlocks the fast version later. Trust the process.
coachingPoints: Widen your stance so the ball can pass through cleanly each rep.
Use your fingertips — not your palm — to guide and push the ball.
Go slow enough that you never lose the ball. Precision before speed.
Switch directions every 30 seconds to train both hands equally.

title: Right Hand Pound Dribble
description: This is your dominant hand's time to get truly dominant. Pounding the ball hard into the floor with your right hand builds wrist strength, timing, and that low, tight dribble that defenders can't poke away. Let's get to work.
coachingPoints: Dribble as low to the ground as possible — ankle height is the goal.
Pound the ball hard. A loud dribble means you're using real force.
Protect the ball with your off hand and body, staying in a wide stance.
Work up to a rhythm of 2 dribbles per second before moving on.

title: Left Hand Pound Dribble
description: Your left hand is your secret weapon — if you train it. Most defenders assume you'll go right, so a strong left hand keeps them honest and opens up the whole court. Embrace the awkward feeling. That's where growth lives.
coachingPoints: It will feel uncomfortable at first — that means it's working. Stay patient.
Match the same intensity and dribble height you use with your right hand.
Keep your elbow low and push through the ball, not slap at it.
Aim for the same rep speed as your strong hand by the end of week two.

title: Crossover at Waist Height
description: The crossover is one of the most dangerous weapons in basketball — but only if you can do it at speed without looking down. Start at a controlled pace to build muscle memory, then push for quicker transitions. Make your crossover automatic.
coachingPoints: Cross at knee-to-waist height — high crossovers are easy to steal.
Push the ball across your body with a snapping wrist motion.
Shift your weight and shoulders with each crossover to simulate a real move.
Work up to a smooth, flowing rhythm before adding hesitation or change of pace.

title: Spider Dribble
description: Four taps around the ball in rapid succession — the Spider Dribble builds hand speed and touch that translates directly to tight ball-handling situations. It looks flashy but it's pure fundamentals underneath. Earn the flash by grinding the basics.
coachingPoints: Pattern: front-right, front-left, back-right, back-left — keep it consistent.
Use only your fingertips and stay light on the ball for maximum hand speed.
Don't rush the pattern. Accuracy first, speed second.
Keep your head and eyes up even though the ball is right in front of you.

title: Between-the-Legs Crossover
description: Taking your dribble through your legs is the next level of ball security and creativity. When it's smooth and low, defenders have no chance of reaching it. Put in the reps and watch this become your most reliable move in traffic.
coachingPoints: Lead with a step forward so your leg creates a gate for the ball to pass through.
Push the ball through from back to front with a sharp wrist snap.
Keep the dribble low — between-the-legs at ankle height is safest.
Alternate legs each rep to develop both sides equally and build rhythm.

title: Behind-the-Back Move
description: The behind-the-back is a game-changer when defenders try to cut off your path. Used at the right moment, it's nearly impossible to steal. This drill locks in the mechanics so the move feels natural under game pressure.
coachingPoints: Wrap the ball around your lower back — not high up near your shoulders.
The receiving hand should already be in position waiting for the ball.
Practice at a slow walk first, then speed up as it becomes natural.
Keep your body upright; don't lean forward or the ball will sail out in front.

title: In-and-Out Move (Both Hands)
description: The in-and-out is one of the most deceptive hesitation moves in the game — it looks like a crossover but stays in the same hand. Sold on both sides, it can freeze any defender. This drill wires in the move so it becomes pure instinct.
coachingPoints: Snap your wrist inward, then quickly redirect outward — the snap sells the fake.
Shift your shoulder inside to complete the sell of the crossover fake.
Practice right-hand in-and-out and left-hand in-and-out as separate sets.
Add a change of pace: slow into the move, then explosive out of it.

title: Cone Zig-Zag Dribble
description: Set up five cones and attack each one like it's a real defender. The zig-zag dribble trains your ability to change direction at speed while keeping your head up and protecting the ball. Set your cones, set your timer, and go.
coachingPoints: Attack each cone low and hard — don't decelerate until you're right on it.
Use a mix of crossovers, between-the-legs, and hesitations at each cone.
Keep your head up so you can see the next cone before you reach the current one.
Push off your outside foot explosively when changing direction.

title: Two-Ball Alternating Pound
description: Level up from stationary two-ball by alternating the timing — when one ball goes down, the other comes up. This drill destroys any remaining hand dependency and builds the independent dribbling ability that makes you a true point guard threat.
coachingPoints: Start with simultaneous dribbles, then shift to alternating once you have rhythm.
Keep both dribbles at the same height and force — no favoring the strong hand.
Eyes up the entire time. Pick a target on the wall and hold focus.
Try moving forward and backward as your control improves.

title: Full-Court Dribble Series
description: Take your handles the full length of the floor and combine every move you've learned. One hand, then the other, then combo moves from baseline to baseline. This is where ball handling meets conditioning — there's nowhere to hide on a full court.
coachingPoints: Assign a different move to each length: right hand, left hand, crossover, between legs.
Sprint the first length at full speed to simulate transition opportunities.
Maintain ball control even when your breathing gets heavy — that's the point.
Finish every length with a layup to close out the move game-realistically.

title: Combo Move Series (5-Move Combo)
description: String five moves together in sequence — crossover, between-the-legs, behind-the-back, hesitation, and step-back — until it flows as one continuous action. Elite ball handlers don't think about individual moves; they just play. This drill builds that autopilot.
coachingPoints: Assign a sequence and memorize it before starting — don't improvise until it's mastered.
Each transition between moves should be seamless; no dead dribbles in between.
Add an explosive burst after the last move to simulate attacking the basket.
Film yourself to identify which move in the chain breaks down under fatigue.

title: Chair Dribble Series
description: A chair as a stationary defender is humbling at first — and that's exactly the point. Working around an obstacle at game speed with your handles tight forces creativity and quickness that open court work simply can't replicate.
coachingPoints: Position the chair at the three-point line and attack it from different angles each set.
Use jab steps before your dribble move to simulate reading a live defender.
Vary your move each rep: don't always go the same direction around the chair.
Finish at the rim after each sequence to add a scoring element to the drill.

title: Two-Ball Crossover + Between the Legs
description: The ultimate two-ball challenge: crossing both balls over simultaneously, then threading them both between your legs. If you can nail this, your hands are ready for anything the game throws at you. Get comfortable being uncomfortable.
coachingPoints: Master two-ball simultaneous crossover before attempting the between-the-legs version.
For the BTL, widen your stance significantly so both balls have a clear path.
Move slowly at first — this drill is about coordination, not speed.
Count your successful consecutive combos to turn it into a personal challenge.

title: Speed Dribble + Euro Step Finish
description: Explode in a straight line, then use the Euro step to sidestep the imaginary shot-blocker and lay it in softly on the other side. This two-step finish is one of the most valuable weapons for guards and forwards who love to attack the paint.
coachingPoints: Plant your first step firmly and use it to redirect your momentum sideways.
Keep the ball protected and low during the gather step.
The second step determines which side you finish on — commit to it.
Practice finishing with both hands; right-side Euro = left-hand finish, and vice versa.

title: Mikan Drill (Full Speed)
description: George Mikan invented this drill because great big men earn their buckets close to the basket. Go up strong on both sides of the rim as fast as you can — no wasted motion, no extra steps. If you can master the Mikan, the paint is your playground.
coachingPoints: Alternate sides continuously — right side, left side, right side — no pauses.
Go up with two hands to protect the ball, then finish with the inside hand.
Jump off the correct foot for each side to build natural footwork habits.
Count your makes in 60 seconds and try to beat your personal record each set.

title: Press Break Solo (Full Court)
description: Imagine you're trapped in a full-court press and you're the only escape route. This drill simulates beating pressure defense with controlled dribbling, directional changes, and smart decision-making — all the way to a finish at the other end.
coachingPoints: Receive the inbound low and immediately attack the center of the floor.
Use your body and change-of-direction moves to split imaginary traps.
Never put yourself in a corner — angle your dribble toward the middle.
Finish with a composed layup or pull-up — simulate end-of-possession scoring.

title: Form Shooting (Close Range)
description: Every great shooter started right here — two feet in front of the basket, one hand, pure form. Form shooting is not a beginner drill; it's what pros do every single day to maintain their mechanics. Own your shot from two feet before you dare move back.
coachingPoints: Use only your shooting hand to guide the ball — off hand does not push the shot.
Bend your knees, load, and extend in one fluid upward motion.
Finish with your wrist snapping down and fingers pointing at the basket.
Watch the ball hit the back of the rim and hold your follow-through until it does.

title: Free Throw Routine
description: Free throws win games — it's that simple. The difference between good and great often comes down to who makes their free throws under pressure. Build a routine, trust it, and make it automatic so the pressure of the moment becomes irrelevant.
coachingPoints: Develop a consistent pre-shot routine: same number of dribbles, same breath, every time.
Align your shooting foot with the nail in the center of the free throw line.
Relax your shoulders and grip — tension is the enemy of a good free throw.
Track your percentage each session. Improvement is the only goal.

title: Catch-and-Shoot (Elbow)
description: The elbow is one of the highest-percentage spots on the floor, and the catch-and-shoot from there is a skill every player at every position must have. Simulate the catch, get your feet under you in one motion, and fire. Repetition builds confidence.
coachingPoints: Catch the ball with your hands already in shooting position — don't adjust after.
Hop into your shooting stance as the ball arrives so you're ready to fire immediately.
Aim for the back of the rim on mid-range shots — this is your target.
Work both elbows equally: right elbow and left elbow for 15 makes each.

title: Bank Shot (45 Degree)
description: The bank shot is an underused weapon that gives you a larger target and bails out shots that are slightly offline. Big men, mid-range players, and smart guards all have a reliable bank shot in their arsenal. Learn the geometry; use the glass.
coachingPoints: From the 45-degree angle, aim for the top corner of the backboard square.
Use the same shooting form — the bank is about your target, not your mechanics.
Shoot with a medium-high arc so the ball comes down into the glass at a good angle.
Track both sides of the floor: work from the right 45 and left 45 equally.

title: Layup Lines (Right + Left)
description: Layups are the highest-percentage shot in basketball and still get missed all the time. Make both hands automatic so that when you're in the open court with a clear lane, the finish is never in question. No excuses on layups.
coachingPoints: Right-side layups: plant left foot, jump off left, lay up with right hand.
Left-side layups: plant right foot, jump off right, lay up with left hand.
Use the backboard on both sides for the highest-percentage finish.
Start at a walk, then jog, then full speed — never compromise form for pace.

title: 5-Spot Shooting
description: Five spots, three makes each, moving clockwise — this is the shooting drill that separates workers from talkers. Hit your spots consistently and your shot becomes a weapon defenders have to respect, which opens up everything else in your game.
coachingPoints: Five spots: left corner, left wing, top of key, right wing, right corner.
Make three at each spot before moving on — misses mean you stay.
Track your total makes-to-attempts ratio to measure improvement over time.
Add a catch-and-shoot simulation at each spot: toss to yourself, hop, fire.

title: Curl Cuts Off Cones
description: Most shots in games come off movement, not standing still. The curl cut off a screen is one of the most common ways shooters get open, and this drill trains the footwork and shooting form to make that split-second shot automatic.
coachingPoints: Use your inside foot to plant and push off tightly around the cone.
Your hands should be up and ready before you receive the ball.
Catch, hop, and shoot in one fluid motion — no extra dribbles.
Run the curl from both sides of the floor to prepare for either direction in a game.

title: Off-Dribble Pull-Up (Elbow)
description: The pull-up jumper is the great equalizer — when your defender plays you tight, you stop, rise, and fire over them. Mastering the off-dribble pull-up from the elbow gives you a deadly mid-range game that opponents simply cannot take away.
coachingPoints: Two hard dribbles toward the elbow, then gather on the third step.
Stop on a two-foot hop to square your body to the basket.
Rise straight up — don't lean back or fade away until you've mastered the straight pull-up.
Work 12 makes from the right elbow, then 12 from the left elbow.

title: Corner 3 Drill
description: The corner three is the shortest three-pointer on the floor and one of the most valuable shots in modern basketball. Whether you're a wing player relocating or a guard spotting up, drilling the corner three is an investment that pays off every single game.
coachingPoints: Square your feet and shoulders toward the basket — alignment is everything.
Keep your balance centered; corner threes go short when you lean forward.
Make 10 in each corner before moving on. Don't shortcut this.
Simulate coming off a sprint to the corner before each shot for game realism.

title: Step-Back Jumper
description: The step-back creates separation where none exists, turning a contested look into a clean jumper with one move. When it's in your bag, defenders can't get comfortably close to you. Train it until the footwork is automatic and the shot is pure.
coachingPoints: Hop backward on two feet simultaneously — don't step back on one foot.
Keep the ball tight at your hip during the step-back so defenders can't reach it.
Land balanced before rising — a wobbly landing leads to a missed shot.
Practice 10 makes from the right side and 10 from the left side.

title: 100 Makes Challenge
description: One hundred makes, any spot, any range — just don't stop until you hit them all. Clock yourself every session and chase your personal best time. This drill builds shooting endurance, mental toughness, and the relentless scorer's mentality.
coachingPoints: Start close and move out as you get warm — don't shoot cold threes from the jump.
Track your time each session to compete against yourself.
Maintain your shooting form even when you're tired — that's the whole test.
Try to string together makes from the same spot before moving to build rhythm.

title: Step-Back 3
description: You've mastered the mid-range step-back — now push it back to the three-point line where the reward is even greater. This is a weapon only for players who've put in elite hours. Defenders will be terrified when they see you receive the ball beyond the arc.
coachingPoints: The step-back must be longer to create enough space from the three-point line.
Add more knee bend and leg drive to get enough power on the extended shot.
10 makes each side — right side 10, then left side 10 to complete the drill.
Film your footwork and compare it to your mid-range step-back — it should look identical.

title: Floater Series (Both Sides)
description: When shot blockers collapse on your layup attempt, the floater is your escape hatch. A well-timed floater at the right arc is nearly unblockable, even against seven-footers. This drill builds the touch, arc, and footwork to make the floater reliable in traffic.
coachingPoints: Release the floater off one foot before the defender can fully contest.
Aim for high arc — the ball should peak well above the rim before dropping in.
Use your body to shield the shot from the side the defender is coming from.
Work 8 makes from the right side, then 7 from the left side for 15 total.

title: Defensive Stance Hold
description: Defense starts with a stance. A proper defensive stance is exhausting to hold — that's the point. Your stance must be strong enough to stop drives, quick enough to close out, and sustainable enough to maintain for a full possession. Earn it by holding it.
coachingPoints: Feet wider than shoulder-width, knees bent at roughly 90 degrees.
Keep your chest up and back flat — no rounding or leaning forward.
Arms out to the side at hip height, ready to deflect passes or contest shots.
Your weight should be on the balls of your feet, not your heels.

title: Slide Slide Closeout
description: Two slides to close the gap, then a high-hands closeout on the shooter. This is one of the most important defensive sequences in the game, and most players do it wrong. Nail the mechanics here and you'll be a defensive asset your team can count on.
coachingPoints: Two quick defensive slides to close distance — never cross your feet.
Chop your steps as you approach the shooter to stay under control.
Hand up high in the shooter's face — not reaching, just contesting.
Land in a defensive stance ready to guard the drive after the contest.

title: Ball-You-Man Shadow
description: Great defenders are always in the right spot. The Ball-You-Man principle means you position yourself so you can see both your man and the ball at all times. This drill trains that awareness through movement so it becomes automatic in games.
coachingPoints: Start in help-side position: one foot in the lane, head on a swivel.
As the 'ball' moves, adjust your position to maintain the ball-you-man line.
Practice with a partner pointing to simulate ball movement, or use cones.
Your goal is to deny easy cuts while staying ready to help on drives.

title: Mirror Drill (Cone)
description: React. React. React. The mirror drill develops the lateral quickness and change-of-direction reaction time that separates good defenders from great ones. Use a cone to simulate the ball-handler's movement and stay in front no matter what.
coachingPoints: Stay in a low defensive stance for the entire drill — no standing up.
Move laterally by sliding your feet; never cross them in front of each other.
React to direction changes by pushing off your outside foot explosively.
The goal is to keep the cone (or partner) in front of you for the entire set.

title: Zig-Zag Slide (Full Court)
description: Full court, baseline to baseline, non-stop lateral slides in a zig-zag pattern. This is the classic defensive conditioning drill that builds both the footwork and the endurance to stay in front of your man for 32 minutes. No shortcuts on this one.
coachingPoints: Stay in your defensive stance for the entire length — don't stand up at the turns.
Touch the sideline with your hand before changing direction.
Lead with your hip, not your shoulder, when changing direction at each line.
Push yourself to slide faster on each subsequent run.

title: Closeout + Contest
description: When the ball swings to your man, you must close out fast and contest the shot — but without fouling or flying by. This drill trains the controlled aggression that makes elite defenders disruptive without being undisciplined.
coachingPoints: Sprint the first two-thirds of the closeout, then chop steps the final third.
Arrive under control with one hand high and the other low to prevent the drive.
Don't jump on shot fakes — read the shooter's eyes and knees, not the ball.
After the contest, find your man's body to box out for the rebound.

title: Pick-and-Roll Defense Series
description: The pick-and-roll is run on almost every possession in modern basketball. Knowing how to navigate screens, communicate with teammates, and recover position is what separates smart defenders from guys who always give up easy buckets. Master the coverage.
coachingPoints: Practice three coverages: hedge, drop, and switch — each has a different purpose.
For the hedge: the big steps up forcefully, then recovers back to his man.
For the drop: the big sags to protect the rim while the guard fights over the screen.
Communication is mandatory — call 'screen left' or 'ball screen' before contact.

title: Box Jumps
description: Explosive power off the ground starts with box jumps. Whether it's going up for a rebound, getting your shot off above a defender, or sprinting in transition, your vertical and first-step quickness begin right here. Jump with purpose every single rep.
coachingPoints: Load into a quarter-squat before each jump — don't start standing straight up.
Swing your arms upward explosively to add momentum to the jump.
Land softly with bent knees to protect your joints and prep for the next jump.
Step down off the box rather than jumping down to save your legs for maximum reps.

title: Lateral Bounds
description: Lateral bounds build the hip strength and single-leg power that drive your defensive slides and first-step quickness on offense. One explosive push off each leg, covering maximum horizontal distance. Your legs are your engine — build them.
coachingPoints: Push hard off your outside foot and drive horizontally, not vertically.
Land on your opposite single foot and hold the landing for one full second before bounding back.
Keep your arms pumping in rhythm to generate momentum.
Try to cover more ground with each session as your power develops.

title: Jump Rope (Basic)
description: Jump rope is the most underrated training tool in basketball. It builds coordination, calf strength, and conditioning simultaneously — and it's available anywhere. Three sets of 60 seconds might seem simple, but do it every day and watch your feet change.
coachingPoints: Stay on the balls of your feet — never let your heels touch the ground.
Keep your elbows close to your sides and turn the rope with your wrists.
Find a rhythm before trying to speed up. Consistency beats speed early on.
Progress to alternating feet, then double-unders as your coordination improves.

title: Sprint + Backpedal (Court Lengths)
description: Sprint one full court length, then backpedal the other way — this simulates the exact transition demands of a real game. Your body needs to know how to accelerate forward and decelerate backward repeatedly without losing form or speed.
coachingPoints: Sprint at 100% effort — if you're not giving everything, you're not training speed.
Transition into the backpedal by opening your hips, not turning all the way around.
Stay low during the backpedal — your defensive stance applies here too.
Recover fully between sets to ensure true maximum effort on each run.

title: Reactive Agility Ladder
description: The agility ladder at elite speed trains your feet to move faster than your brain thinks possible. This reactive version — where you respond to verbal or visual cues for each pattern — takes it a level above standard ladder work and simulates real game demands.
coachingPoints: Work through at least three patterns: two-in, lateral shuffle, and Icky shuffle.
Have a partner call direction changes mid-ladder to add the reactive element.
Stay on your toes the entire time — heel contact slows you down dramatically.
Record your ladder time and push to break your personal best on each session.

title: Approach Vertical Jumps
description: Your standing vertical is one thing — but your approach vertical, with a two-step gather and explosive jump, is what actually matters at the rim. This drill trains the exact jump mechanics used for dunks, layups, and contested shots.
coachingPoints: Two powerful approach steps, then a penultimate step to gather your jump.
Drive your inside knee upward explosively to maximize jump height.
Reach maximum extension at the top — stretch for the highest target possible.
Land on two feet in a balanced position to prepare for your next action.

title: 17s (Suicide-Style Timed Drill)
description: 17 sideline-to-sideline sprints in under 60 seconds. This is the conditioning benchmark used by real varsity and college programs to test who wants it and who doesn't. It's brutal. It's supposed to be. The players who can finish the 17s are the ones who show up in the fourth quarter.
coachingPoints: Touch the sideline with your hand each time — no half-touches.
Maintain your form even in the final three sprints when your body is screaming.
Breathe out on exertion; don't hold your breath during the sprints.
Rest 2 full minutes between each of the three sets to ensure true maximum effort.

title: Jab Step Series
description: One jab step separates a great offensive player from a confused one. The jab forces the defender to commit, and then you attack the gap they leave. This series trains all three reads: jab and drive, jab and shoot, jab and reset. Own the triple threat.
coachingPoints: Start in a strong triple-threat position: balanced, ball at your hip, eyes up.
Jab with your non-pivot foot 12-18 inches in any direction to create a read.
React to the imaginary defender: if they step back, shoot; if they bite, drive.
Practice the jab-and-go, jab-and-pull-up, and jab-and-reset as three separate sets.

title: Pivot Footwork (Front + Reverse)
description: Being able to pivot without traveling is a fundamental skill that players take for granted — until they get called for travels in big moments. Master both the front pivot and the reverse pivot and your footwork will be clean enough to survive any referee.
coachingPoints: Establish your pivot foot clearly on every catch — it cannot slide or lift.
Front pivot: swing your non-pivot foot forward to face a new direction.
Reverse pivot: swing your non-pivot foot backward to turn away from pressure.
Practice both pivots from both feet to prepare for any situation in a game.

title: V-Cut Reading
description: The V-cut is how you get open without the ball — and getting open is the first skill of every great scorer. This drill trains the sharp change of direction, the burst to space, and the ready hands that let you receive the ball in rhythm and be a threat immediately.
coachingPoints: Walk your defender low toward the basket, then explode upward to the wing or top.
Time the cut so you arrive as the ball arrives — not too early, not too late.
Hands up and target hand extended to give the passer a clear aim point.
After receiving, immediately read the defense: can you shoot, drive, or need to pass?

title: Screen Setting Footwork
description: A good screen makes your whole team better. A bad screen — moving, angled wrong, or set too early — gets called every time and kills possessions. This drill trains the footwork to set a legal, effective screen that creates real advantages for your team.
coachingPoints: Sprint to the screening position and stop completely — no moving feet when setting.
Make your screen body as wide as possible: feet shoulder-width, arms crossed at chest.
Angle your screen to funnel the defender in the direction your teammate wants to go.
After the screen, immediately roll to the basket or pop to the perimeter based on your read.

title: Read-the-Defense Flash
description: Flashing to the high post or mid-post at the right moment — and knowing what to do with the ball when you receive it — is what separates high-IQ players from scorers who can only play in isolation. Read, flash, receive, and make the right decision every time.
coachingPoints: Read the weak side first before flashing — is the lane clear or occupied?
Flash with intent: slow-to-fast movement with a hard target hand.
On the catch, immediately read the defense: one-on-one, dump off, or shoot?
Practice all three outcomes from the flash position in each set.

title: Pin-Down + Flare Reads
description: The pin-down screen followed by the flare option is advanced off-ball movement that advanced defenses struggle to account for. When your defender overplays one option, you hit them with the other. This drill builds the reads to always make the right call.
coachingPoints: Read the defender's position as you approach the screen: tight or sagging?
Tight defender: use the curl cut under the screen for a close-range shot.
Sagging defender: flare away from the screen for an open three-pointer.
Practice both reads in each set — don't just run the one you're comfortable with.
